rooms: Street dances in neighborhoods with no dancehalls or concert spaces
sound: Truck-borne rigs with generators and wardrobe-sized speaker cabinets; a selector on the records, a DJ toasting, and one-off dubplates as the draw.
credit: Working-class Kingston crews, among them Tom the Great Sebastian (Tom Wong), Duke Reid's Trojan, Coxsone Dodd's Downbeat and King Tubby's Hometown Hi-Fi.

rooms: Carnival street corners, such as Channel One's at Leamington Road Villas since 1983
sound: Static sound systems played in the street, which the 1973 organizer Leslie Palmer called "the voice of the youth".
credit: London's Caribbean community: Claudia Jones, Rhaune Laslett and Leslie Palmer as organizers, Linett Kamala as carnival's first female DJ, and Mellotone as its first all-female sound system.

sound: Sound designed first: Alex Rosner at the Loft, Richard Long with Larry Levan at the Garage; no alcohol, so parties ran until noon.
credit: Black and Latino, largely gay dancers; David Mancuso, Larry Levan and the Garage's members, a crowd the NYC LGBT Historic Sites Project describes as "primarily African-American gay men".

rooms: The Warehouse, the Music Box, the Power Plant
sound: A Richard Long system you could hear from the street, the booth on the loading dock, a dark room with fog, then cheap Roland drum machines and WBMX radio mixes.
credit: Black gay men and women and Latino dancers first; Robert Williams, Frankie Knuckles, Ron Hardy, the Hot Mix 5 and producers such as Phuture.

rooms: High-school "prep" party circuit, the Music Institute at 1315 Broadway
sound: Machine-made tracks on artist-run labels such as Metroplex, later with Underground Resistance's anonymity and anti-corporate stance.
credit: Young Black musicians from the Detroit area, led by Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, then "Mad" Mike Banks and Jeff Mills.

rooms: Shoom, Future, Spectrum, The Trip, then warehouses and fields
sound: Warehouse and field parties promoted by flyer, word of mouth and pager, playing Chicago and Detroit records.
credit: Danny and Jenni Rampling, Paul Oakenfold, Nicky Holloway and Johnny Walker after hearing Alfredo on Ibiza, and raves such as Sunrise, Energy and Biology.

rooms: Commons and fields, most famously Castlemorton Common
sound: Collective-run sound systems at multi-day unlicensed gatherings.
credit: Sound system collectives including Spiral Tribe, Bedlam, Circus Warp and DiY.

rooms: AWOL, Roast, Telepathy; pirate station Kool FM
sound: Breakbeats under ragga basslines and sound system samples, carried by MCs, pirates and sub-bass rigs.
credit: Black British sound system culture and the scene's DJs, MCs and pirate broadcasters.

rooms: Pirate stations such as Rinse FM and Deja Vu
sound: MCs and pirate radio, working under pressure from the police risk-assessment Form 696.
credit: East London MCs and producers, with Dizzee Rascal's Mercury Prize in 2003.

rooms: FWD>> at the Velvet Rooms and Plastic People; DMZ in Brixton
sound: Sub-bass weight traced to the Jamaican sound system party scene.
credit: FWD>>, Croydon's Big Apple Records, Digital Mystikz and Loefah.

sound: Repurposed vaults and power plants, phone and photo policies as atmosphere, and close ties to Detroit through Tresor Records.
credit: Dimitri Hegemann and the Tresor team, Detroit artists on the label, and the queer fetish party culture behind Berghain.

sound: Open-air terrace clubs and eclectic all-night sets mixing house with disco, rock, jazz, funk, soul and synth pop.
credit: Alfredo Fiorito, born in Rosario, Argentina, the resident who defined Balearic beat.

rooms: Beach and forest parties; later Boom in Portugal
sound: Two tape decks, then DAT, at outdoor parties; later decor-led, multi-day stages with sunrise sets and harm-reduction spaces.
credit: DJs such as Goa Gil, Fred Disko and Laurent, then London nights such as Return to the Source.

rooms: Clubs including the Ancienne Belgique and Boccaccio, depending on the account
sound: Records slowed down on the deck, by the usual story a 45 played at 33 rpm with the pitch at +8.
credit: Belgian club DJs; accounts credit Dikke Ronny or Marc Grouls, and the origin story is unverified.

sound: Hardcore records with an explicit anti-racist stance against far-right attempts to claim the scene.
credit: Rotterdam's hardcore scene, including Paul Elstak, DJ Chosen Few and Party Animals.

rooms: Stadium-scale festivals such as Electric Daisy Carnival
sound: Rave-derived festivals repackaged as rock-style shows with a pop-oriented, big-room sound.
credit: The US music industry and festival promoters, building on decades of earlier scenes.

sound: The log drum, linked to the kwaito pioneer M'du Masilela.
credit: Gauteng's DJs and producers, with no single founder.

rooms: Neighborhood parties in areas such as Tepito
sound: Sound systems playing cumbia, salsa and guaracha while the sonidero sends saludos over the music.
credit: Mexico City's sonidero crews and the migrant communities who carried the culture north.
